courses.title: Mastering Electric Principles
moduleTitles: Elements That Every Circuit Must Have
Understanding Circuit Protection Series and Partial Circuits

questions.prompt: In conventional current flow theory, current is said to flow:
questions.explanation: Conventional flow is described as positive to negative through the external circuit; electron flow is the opposite direction.

options.label: A
options.body: From negative to positive through the load

options.label: B
options.body: From positive to negative through the external circuit

options.label: D
options.body: From ground directly to the load

questions.prompt: An atom with electrons that move easily between atoms is best described as:
questions.explanation: Conductors have free electrons that move easily, allowing current flow.

questions.prompt: According to Ohm's Law, if voltage stays the same and resistance doubles, current will:
questions.explanation: I = V / R, so doubling R at fixed V halves current.

questions.prompt: A 12 V circuit has 4 ohms of resistance. How much current flows?
In the water analogy for electricity, water pressure is most like:
questions.explanation: Pressure pushes water as voltage pushes charge through a circuit.

questions.prompt: In the water analogy, a partly closed valve that restricts flow is most like:
questions.explanation: Restriction to flow models resistance restricting current.

options.label: D
options.body: Voltage drop only at the source

questions.prompt: A bulb draws 2 A from a 12 V supply. Its resistance is:
questions.explanation: R = V / I = 12 / 2 = 6 ohms.

questions.prompt: A motor uses 120 W on a 12 V system. Approximately how much current does it draw?
Which set lists elements every complete circuit must have?
questions.moduleTitle: Elements That Every Circuit Must Have
questions.explanation: A working circuit needs a power source, protection, a load, conductors and a return path, usually with control.

options.label: A
options.body: Source, protection, load and return path

options.label: B
options.body: Only a battery and a switch

questions.prompt: In a series circuit, if one load opens, what happens?
questions.moduleTitle: Understanding Circuit Protection Series and Partial Circuits
questions.explanation: A series path has one route for current, so an open stops current everywhere in that path.

options.label: B
options.body: Current stops through the whole series path

courses.title: Essential Multimeter Skills
moduleTitles: Measuring Amps and Volts and Resistance

questions.prompt: To measure voltage, the meter leads are connected:
questions.explanation: A voltmeter connects in parallel across the part being measured.

options.label: B
options.body: In parallel across the component or circuit

options.label: C
options.body: With power off across a fuse only

options.label: D
options.body: Red to ground only, black removed

questions.prompt: Before measuring resistance on a component, you should:
questions.explanation: Resistance is measured on an unpowered, preferably isolated component, or readings will be wrong and the meter may be damaged.

options.label: B
options.body: Disconnect power and isolate the component where needed

questions.prompt: To measure current with a standard multimeter, the meter is placed:
questions.moduleTitle: Measuring Amps and Volts and Resistance
questions.explanation: Current measurement puts the meter in series so circuit current flows through it, within its rating.

questions.prompt: A meter on the 20 V DC scale reads 12.6 on a resting battery. This indicates:
questions.moduleTitle: Measuring Amps and Volts and Resistance
questions.explanation: About 12.6 V at rest is the expected fully charged lead-acid battery voltage.

options.label: D
options.body: An open cell in every case

questions.prompt: When checking resistance, infinite or OL on the display most likely means:
questions.moduleTitle: Measuring Amps and Volts and Resistance
questions.explanation: OL means overload/open - no measurable continuity within the selected range.

options.label: B
options.body: An open circuit or resistance beyond the range

questions.prompt: Duty cycle describes:
questions.explanation: Duty cycle is on-time as a percentage of the total cycle time.

options.label: B
options.body: The percentage of time a signal is on during one cycle

questions.prompt: A PWM solenoid at 75% duty cycle is:
questions.explanation: 75% duty means energised for 75% of each cycle.

questions.prompt: If frequency increases but duty cycle stays the same, what happens?
questions.explanation: Higher frequency shortens cycle time; the percentage on stays the same.

options.label: A
options.body: Each cycle gets shorter, but the on proportion stays the same

questions.prompt: In diode test mode, a good silicon diode tested in forward bias typically shows about:
questions.explanation: A silicon diode drops roughly 0.5-0.7 V when forward biased.

questions.prompt: A continuity beeper sounding does NOT by itself prove:
questions.explanation: Continuity only shows a path exists; a single strand can beep yet drop voltage badly under load.

options.label: A
options.body: The path has very high resistance

options.label: B
options.body: The circuit can carry full load current without voltage drop

options.label: C
options.body: The fuse is the correct rating

courses.title: Advanced Multimeter Skills
moduleTitles: Getting the Most From a Multimeter

questions.prompt: Using a meter's MIN/MAX recording is most useful for:
questions.moduleTitle: Getting the Most From a Multimeter
questions.explanation: MIN/MAX captures the lowest and highest values seen during monitoring, helping find intermittents.

options.label: B
options.body: Catching intermittent voltage drops or glitches over time

questions.prompt: Why select a manual range instead of autoranging during a fast-changing test?
questions.moduleTitle: Getting the Most From a Multimeter
questions.explanation: Fixing the range stops the meter hunting between ranges while the value changes quickly.

options.label: B
options.body: Manual range avoids range-hunting delays and unstable readings

questions.prompt: A low-impedance meter mode is preferred when checking for unwanted 'ghost' voltage because it:
questions.moduleTitle: Getting the Most From a Multimeter
questions.explanation: Low impedance loads the circuit, so capacitively coupled ghost voltage disappears while real supply remains.

options.label: B
options.body: Loads the circuit slightly so induced voltage collapses

questions.prompt: Relative (REL) mode is used to:
questions.moduleTitle: Getting the Most From a Multimeter
questions.explanation: REL subtracts a reference, such as lead resistance, from later readings.

options.label: A
options.body: Zero out lead resistance or a reference value

questions.prompt: When measuring a small parasitic draw, the best practice is to:
questions.moduleTitle: Getting the Most From a Multimeter
questions.explanation: Keeping the circuit intact with a clamp or shunt avoids waking modules and losing settings.

options.label: A
options.body: Open the circuit suddenly and lose module memory settings where avoidable

options.label: B
options.body: Use an inductive clamp or a shunt method that keeps the circuit powered while modules sleep

questions.prompt: A meter with True RMS is important when measuring:
questions.explanation: True RMS gives accurate AC readings on distorted or non-sine waveforms.

questions.prompt: Frequency measurement on a multimeter reports:
questions.explanation: Frequency is measured in hertz, the number of cycles per second.

questions.prompt: A bar graph on a digital meter helps the technician to:
questions.explanation: The fast-updating bar graph shows trends and flicker the numeric display misses.

options.label: A
options.body: See rapid fluctuations that digits update too slowly to show

questions.prompt: Using a temperature probe with a multimeter is useful for:
questions.explanation: Temperature comparison finds restrictions, poor connections and cooling faults.

options.label: A
options.body: Checking a thermostat, radiator or connector for abnormal heating

questions.prompt: Capacitance mode on a multimeter should be used:
questions.explanation: Capacitors must be discharged and isolated before capacitance testing for safety and accuracy.

options.label: D
options.body: Instead of a scope for all waveforms

courses.title: Diagnosing Circuit Faults
moduleTitles: Using Voltage Drops as an Electrical Diagnostic Tool

questions.prompt: A short to ground before the load will most likely:
questions.explanation: A pre-load short to ground creates excessive current, opening the fuse or protection.

options.label: A
options.body: Reduce voltage drop across the load to normal

options.label: B
options.body: Blow the fuse or trip protection

options.label: D
options.body: Increase resistance in a controlled way

questions.prompt: An open circuit is best defined as:
questions.explanation: An open is a break in the path so current cannot flow.

options.label: B
options.body: A break that stops current flow in the path

options.label: C
options.body: A path to ground after the load

questions.prompt: Back probing a sealed connector is preferred to piercing insulation because it:
questions.explanation: Back probing tests the circuit without breaking insulation and inviting corrosion.

questions.prompt: Poor terminal tension (drag) can cause:
questions.explanation: Loose terminals make poor contact, causing intermittents, voltage drop and heat.

options.label: B
options.body: Intermittent opens and heat at the connection

questions.prompt: The preferred repair for a critical harness wire is generally:
questions.explanation: A sealed solder or crimp splice restores strength, conductivity and corrosion protection.

options.label: B
options.body: Solder or sealed crimp splice with heat-shrink, following manufacturer guidance

options.label: D
options.body: Leave strands cut if most remain

questions.prompt: A wiggle test while monitoring a meter or scope helps to:
questions.explanation: Moving the harness while watching readings exposes movement-sensitive faults.

options.label: B
options.body: Reveal intermittent opens or shorts when the harness moves

questions.prompt: Voltage drop is:
questions.explanation: Voltage drop is the voltage consumed across resistance while current flows.

options.label: A
options.body: Voltage used as current passes through resistance in a loaded circuit

options.label: B
options.body: Battery voltage with everything off only

options.label: D
options.body: The same as an open circuit voltage reading

questions.prompt: Voltage drop testing must be done:
questions.explanation: No current means no meaningful voltage drop, so the circuit must be loaded and operating.

options.label: A
options.body: With the circuit off and disconnected

options.label: B
options.body: With the circuit operating under load

questions.prompt: On a 5 V sensor signal circuit, an unwanted drop is most concerning because:
questions.explanation: Low-current signal circuits need accuracy; even small unwanted drops distort sensor information.

options.label: A
options.body: Signal circuits carry high starter current

options.label: B
options.body: Small drops represent a large percentage error in the signal

options.label: C
options.body: It only affects the ground side

questions.prompt: A ground side voltage drop of 0.8 V on a cranking circuit indicates:
questions.moduleTitle: Using Voltage Drops as an Electrical Diagnostic Tool
questions.explanation: A high ground drop under load points to resistance in cables, connections or ground points.

options.label: B
options.body: Excessive resistance in the ground path

options.label: C
options.body: Low battery state of charge only

questions.prompt: When selecting replacement cable, the most important factors are:
questions.explanation: Cable must carry the current over its length and suit heat, oil and abrasion conditions.

options.label: B
options.body: Current capacity, length, insulation and environment

options.label: D
options.body: Diameter of the connector shell only

questions.prompt: A cable run near exhaust heat requires:
questions.explanation: Heat-rated insulation prevents melting, shorting and premature failure.

options.label: B
options.body: Insulation rated for the higher temperature

questions.prompt: If a circuit's cable is too thin for its length and current, the result is:
questions.explanation: Undersized cable has more resistance, causing drop and heat under load.

options.label: D
options.body: No effect if the fuse is large

questions.prompt: Doubling a cable's length, with the same gauge and current, will:
questions.explanation: Longer conductors have more resistance, so drop increases.

options.label: B
options.body: Increase total resistance and voltage drop

questions.prompt: A correct crimp should:
questions.explanation: A good crimp is gas-tight, mechanically strong and does not damage strands.

options.label: A
options.body: Cut most strands for a tight fit

options.label: B
options.body: Compress the terminal evenly, gripping conductor and insulation support without cutting strands

questions.prompt: The pull test after crimping checks:
questions.explanation: A gentle pull confirms the terminal is securely attached.

options.label: B
options.body: Mechanical strength of the crimp joint

questions.prompt: A sealed automotive connector's weather seals are there to:
questions.explanation: Seals protect against water ingress and corrosion at the connection.

options.label: B
options.body: Keep moisture and contamination out of the terminal area

questions.prompt: A terminal position assurance (TPA) lock does what?
questions.explanation: TPA secondary locks keep terminals from backing out.

options.label: B
options.body: Confirms and holds terminals fully seated in the housing

questions.prompt: In soldering, flux is used to:
questions.explanation: Flux removes oxides so solder bonds properly to the conductors.

options.label: B
options.body: Clean oxides and help solder flow and wet the metals

questions.prompt: A dull, grainy solder joint that moved while cooling is called a:
questions.explanation: Movement or insufficient heat makes a weak, high-resistance cold joint.

options.label: A
options.body: Cold / dry joint, and it should be remade

questions.prompt: A relay allows:
questions.explanation: The coil (low current) controls contacts that switch the high-current load circuit.

options.label: A
options.body: A high-current circuit to be controlled by a low-current switch or module

options.label: B
options.body: Voltage to be created without a source

options.label: D
options.body: A fuse to be bypassed safely

questions.prompt: On a typical ISO relay, terminals 85 and 86 are:
questions.explanation: 85 and 86 are the relay coil connections.

questions.prompt: On a typical 4-pin relay, terminal 30 is commonly:
questions.explanation: Terminal 30 is the common contact, usually the power feed to the contacts.

questions.prompt: When the coil is energised on a normally open relay, terminals 30 and 87:
questions.explanation: Energising the coil closes 30 to 87 on a normally open relay.

questions.prompt: A relay that clicks but the load does not work could have:
questions.explanation: Clicking proves coil operation, not that the contacts carry current cleanly.

options.label: D
options.body: A charged battery in every case

questions.prompt: Testing a relay circuit is best done by checking:
questions.explanation: All four legs - control and load sides - must be verified, ideally loaded.

options.label: A
options.body: Coil feed, coil ground/control, contact feed and output under load

questions.prompt: A suppression diode or resistor across a relay coil is used to:
questions.explanation: Suppression protects electronics from the inductive kickback when the coil de-energises.

options.label: B
options.body: Control the voltage spike when the coil switches off

questions.prompt: In a monitored relay circuit, the control module can detect a fault by:
questions.explanation: Modules monitor feedback voltage or current and set a fault if it does not match the commanded state.

options.label: B
options.body: Watching expected voltage/current feedback on the circuit

questions.prompt: If a module commands a relay on but sees no voltage change on the monitor line, it will likely:
questions.explanation: A mismatch between command and feedback triggers diagnostic trouble codes and possibly a fallback.

questions.prompt: An open in a monitored relay's coil circuit would be detected as:
questions.explanation: The module expects current or a voltage change; an open prevents it and is flagged.

options.label: B
options.body: No coil current / incorrect feedback when commanded

questions.prompt: A headlamp circuit fault causing one dim lamp most often points to:
questions.explanation: One dim lamp usually means voltage drop or a poor ground in that branch.

options.label: A
options.body: High resistance or poor ground on that lamp's circuit

options.label: B
options.body: Excess alternator voltage for all lamps

questions.prompt: Daytime running lights are intended to:
questions.explanation: DRLs improve daytime conspicuity, often at reduced intensity.

options.label: B
options.body: Make the vehicle more visible during the day

options.label: C
options.body: Increase battery drain as a test

questions.prompt: A halogen bulb should not be touched with bare fingers because:
questions.explanation: Skin oils cause uneven heating of the quartz envelope and early failure.

options.label: B
options.body: Oils create hot spots that shorten bulb life

questions.prompt: In an incandescent bulb, light is produced by:
questions.explanation: Current heats the filament to incandescence.

options.label: B
options.body: Heating a filament until it glows

questions.prompt: HID lamps produce light by:
questions.explanation: HID uses an arc discharge, requiring a ballast/igniter for high starting voltage.

options.label: B
options.body: An electric arc through xenon gas and metal salts

questions.prompt: The ballast in an HID system is needed to:
questions.explanation: The ballast/igniter starts the arc and controls current once lit.

options.label: B
options.body: Provide high ignition voltage and then regulate lamp current

questions.prompt: A key advantage of LED lighting is:
questions.explanation: LEDs are efficient, durable and switch instantly, though they need proper drivers and heat management.

options.label: A
options.body: High heat at the lens in all designs

options.label: B
options.body: Low current draw, long life and instant on

options.label: C
options.body: It never needs a driver circuit

options.label: D
options.body: It works with any voltage without control

questions.prompt: If polarity is reversed to a standard LED lamp, it will typically:
questions.explanation: LEDs are diodes, so reverse polarity blocks normal operation.

options.label: B
options.body: Not light, because LEDs allow current in one direction

options.label: D
options.body: Blow every fuse instantly in all cases

questions.prompt: Laser headlights actually produce white light visible on the road by:
questions.explanation: Laser diodes stimulate a phosphor, producing bright white light with safety controls.

options.label: A
options.body: Shining a raw blue laser directly with no conversion

options.label: B
options.body: Using laser diodes to excite a phosphor that emits white light

questions.prompt: Compared with LED, a main claimed benefit of laser high beam is:
questions.explanation: Laser systems achieve long range from a compact source, usually supplementing LED high beam.

options.label: B
options.body: Longer range from a very small, intense light source

questions.prompt: A thermistor used for temperature sensing changes what with temperature?
questions.explanation: Thermistors change resistance with temperature; most automotive ones are NTC.

questions.prompt: An NTC thermistor's resistance as temperature rises:
questions.explanation: Negative temperature coefficient means resistance falls as temperature rises.

questions.prompt: A piezo resistive sensor works because applied pressure:
questions.explanation: Strain changes the resistance of the sensing element, converted to a signal voltage.

options.label: A
options.body: Changes the resistance of a silicon diaphragm element

questions.prompt: MAP and many pressure sensors using piezo resistive elements typically output:
questions.explanation: Pressure changes the bridge output voltage in proportion to pressure.

options.label: A
options.body: A varying analogue voltage proportional to pressure

options.label: D
options.body: A fixed 12 V at all pressures

questions.prompt: A piezo electric sensor differs because it:
questions.explanation: Piezoelectric materials generate charge under stress, ideal for knock and dynamic events.

options.label: A
options.body: Generates a charge/voltage when mechanically stressed

options.label: B
options.body: Needs no movement or vibration ever to produce a signal

options.label: C
options.body: Measures only static pressure perfectly with no decay

questions.prompt: A knock sensor is a common example of:
questions.explanation: Knock sensors use piezoelectric elements to convert vibration into a voltage signal.

questions.prompt: Capacitive sensing detects change in:
questions.explanation: Movement or material change alters capacitance, which electronics convert to a signal.

options.label: B
options.body: Capacitance as distance or dielectric changes

questions.prompt: Capacitive sensors are commonly used for:
questions.explanation: Capacitance suits non-contact level, occupancy and proximity detection.

options.label: B
options.body: Occupant detection, fluid level and touch/proximity sensing

questions.prompt: Ultrasonic parking sensors measure distance by:
questions.explanation: Distance is calculated from the time of flight of the reflected ultrasonic pulse.

options.label: A
options.body: Timing an echo of a high-frequency sound pulse

questions.prompt: A dirty or ice-covered ultrasonic sensor may cause:
questions.explanation: Contamination blocks or distorts the pulse, causing unreliable detection.

courses.title: Master Control Modules
moduleTitles: Pull Up and Pull Down Circuits

questions.prompt: A voltage divider with two equal resistors fed by 10 V will have about how much at the midpoint?
questions.explanation: Equal resistors split the supply equally, giving half at the junction.

questions.prompt: Many sensor circuits work as voltage dividers where the sensor changes:
questions.explanation: As sensor resistance changes, the divider ratio and signal voltage change.

options.label: B
options.body: Resistance, changing the signal voltage the module reads

questions.prompt: In a pull-up circuit, the module's internal resistor pulls the signal:
questions.moduleTitle: Pull Up and Pull Down Circuits
questions.explanation: The pull-up holds the line high until the device pulls it toward ground.

options.label: B
options.body: Toward reference voltage, and the sensor/switch pulls it down

questions.prompt: In a pull-down circuit, with the switch open the signal at the module is typically:
questions.moduleTitle: Pull Up and Pull Down Circuits
questions.explanation: A pull-down resistor holds the input low until a device pulls it high.

questions.prompt: If a pull-up type sensor circuit is shorted to ground, the signal will read:
questions.moduleTitle: Pull Up and Pull Down Circuits
questions.explanation: A short to ground overcomes the pull-up and holds the signal low.

questions.prompt: A control module makes decisions by following the pattern:
questions.explanation: Modules read inputs, process them using logic/maps, then command outputs.

questions.prompt: After replacing certain modules, what may be required before the vehicle works correctly?
questions.explanation: Many modules need software, VIN/configuration coding and relearns.

options.label: B
options.body: Programming, coding and/or configuration to the vehicle

questions.prompt: A module that loses its ground may cause:
questions.explanation: Poor power or ground makes module behaviour erratic and can affect a whole network.

options.label: B
options.body: Multiple unrelated-looking faults and communication errors

questions.prompt: Pass-through programming (J2534 style) means:
questions.explanation: software A pass-through interface lets a PC and OEM software reprogram modules via the DLC.

options.label: A
options.body: Programming a module through the diagnostic connector using a pass-through device and manufacturer software

options.label: B
options.body: Passing a wire through a bulkhead

options.label: D
options.body: Using a test light as a module

questions.prompt: During module programming, the most critical supply requirement is:
questions.explanation: Voltage must stay stable throughout programming or the module can be corrupted.

options.label: B
options.body: Stable battery voltage maintained with a suitable power supply

questions.prompt: On an oscilloscope, the vertical axis represents:
questions.explanation: Vertical is voltage (amplitude); horizontal is time.

questions.prompt: If the time base is set too slow for a fast signal, the waveform may:
questions.explanation: A slow time base squeezes cycles together so detail is hidden.

questions.prompt: Current limiting in a driver circuit protects it by:
questions.explanation: Limiting protects module drivers from overheating on overload or short.

options.label: B
options.body: Capping current to a safe level if a load shorts or overloads

questions.prompt: Pulse width modulation controls average power by:
questions.explanation: Changing duty cycle changes average voltage/current delivered to the load.

options.label: B
options.body: Varying the on-time / duty cycle of a fixed-frequency signal

questions.prompt: A Hall-effect crank position sensor normally produces:
questions.explanation: Hall sensors switch digitally, giving a square wave.

options.label: A
options.body: A clean square-wave switching between low and high

options.label: B
options.body: A sine wave growing with speed only

options.label: D
options.body: A random noise pattern when good

questions.prompt: An inductive (variable reluctance) crank sensor produces:
questions.explanation: VR sensors generate AC; faster rotation means higher frequency and amplitude.

options.label: A
options.body: A square wave of constant height

options.label: B
options.body: An AC sine-like wave whose amplitude and frequency rise with speed

questions.prompt: A missing or distorted tooth gap in a crank waveform will affect:
questions.explanation: The gap is the reference; distortion can cause sync and misfire faults.

options.label: B
options.body: The module's ability to locate crank position / TDC reference

questions.prompt: An in-cylinder pressure waveform can reveal:
questions.explanation: Pressure traces show compression, power, exhaust and intake events.

options.label: B
options.body: Valve timing, sealing and pumping problems from pressure changes

questions.prompt: On a primary ignition waveform, the dwell section is when:
questions.explanation: Dwell is coil-on time, building the magnetic field and primary current.

options.label: A
options.body: The coil is switched off and spark occurs

options.label: B
options.body: Current is building in the coil primary

questions.prompt: On a secondary waveform, a very high firing line with a short burn line can indicate:
questions.explanation: High resistance demands higher firing voltage and leaves less energy for spark duration.

options.label: A
options.body: A rich, easy-to-fire mixture in all cases

options.label: B
options.body: High secondary resistance such as a wide plug gap or open lead

questions.prompt: Relative compression testing compares cylinders by watching:
questions.explanation: Each compression stroke loads the starter; a weak cylinder draws less current.

options.label: A
options.body: Starter current draw or battery voltage dip as each cylinder comes up on compression

questions.prompt: Relative compression is performed during:
questions.explanation: The engine is cranked without starting so starter load reflects compression.

options.label: B
options.body: Cranking with fuelling/ignition disabled as directed

questions.prompt: On a starter-current relative compression trace, a noticeably lower current peak for one cylinder suggests:
questions.explanation: Less compression means less starter load, so a smaller current hump.

options.label: A
options.body: That cylinder has higher compression than the others

options.label: B
options.body: That cylinder has lower compression than the others

options.label: D
options.body: Normal variation that proves a valve fault by itself

questions.prompt: A sync signal (for example cylinder 1 ignition or injection) is used during relative compression to:
questions.explanation: Sync links each peak in firing order to a specific cylinder.

options.label: B
options.body: Identify which peak belongs to which cylinder

questions.prompt: Relative compression tells you:
questions.explanation: It is a comparison test; a low cylinder needs follow-up testing for cause and absolute value.

options.label: A
options.body: The exact psi of each cylinder

options.label: B
options.body: How cylinders compare with each other, not absolute pressure

options.label: C
options.body: The cause of low compression by itself

questions.prompt: Before a relative compression test, an important check is:
questions.explanation: A weak battery or starter distorts the pattern and can mimic compression differences.

options.label: A
options.body: That the battery and starter circuit are in good condition and fully charged

options.label: B
options.body: That the fuel tank is empty

options.label: D
options.body: That the AC is on full

questions.prompt: If ALL cylinders show evenly low starter current humps, suspect:
questions.explanation: A uniform pattern points to a common cause rather than one cylinder.

options.label: B
options.body: A generally weak battery/starter, incorrect cranking speed, or a global engine issue - not one cylinder

questions.prompt: A follow-up test after finding one low cylinder on relative compression is:
questions.explanation: Wet/dry compression and leakage testing locate rings, valves or gasket leakage.

options.label: B
options.body: A conventional compression test and/or cylinder leakage test on that cylinder

questions.prompt: Using battery voltage (instead of a current clamp) for relative compression works because:
questions.explanation: Higher starter load pulls battery voltage down, creating a corresponding voltage trace.

options.label: B
options.body: Battery voltage dips as starter load rises on each compression stroke

questions.prompt: Disabling fuel and ignition before cranking for the test is important to:
questions.explanation: Preventing a start keeps cranking even and safe for comparison.

options.label: A
options.body: Stop the engine starting and to get a clean, even cranking pattern

questions.prompt: In a flooded lead-acid battery, the electrolyte is:
questions.explanation: Flooded lead-acid cells use sulphuric acid electrolyte covering lead plates.

options.label: D
options.body: Lithium polymer gel in every case

questions.prompt: A fully charged flooded cell has a specific gravity of about:
questions.explanation: Around 1.265-1.280 at reference temperature indicates full charge.

questions.prompt: A key difference of lithium 12 V / EV batteries compared with lead-acid is:
questions.explanation: Lithium chemistry needs BMS protection against overcharge, over-discharge and thermal issues.

options.label: A
options.body: They need no management at all

options.label: B
options.body: They require a battery management system to monitor cell voltage, temperature and current

options.label: C
options.body: They use sulphuric acid and lead only

questions.prompt: Lithium batteries generally offer, for the same capacity:
questions.explanation: Lithium packs store more energy per kilogram.

options.label: B
options.body: Lower weight and higher energy density

questions.prompt: A conductance battery test estimates:
questions.explanation: Conductance testing infers health and CCA capability without a full load test.

options.label: B
options.body: Battery capacity / cranking ability from its internal conductance

questions.prompt: Before load testing a battery, you should ensure it is:
questions.explanation: Testing a discharged or badly connected battery gives misleading failures.

options.label: B
options.body: Reasonably charged and terminals are clean and tight

options.label: D
options.body: Filled with tap water to the top

questions.prompt: A parasitic drain test is performed:
questions.explanation: Normal sleep current is measured after the vehicle fully powers down.

options.label: A
options.body: With all modules awake and doors being opened repeatedly

options.label: B
options.body: After modules have gone to sleep, measuring key-off current draw

options.label: D
options.body: With the engine at full revs

questions.prompt: To locate which circuit causes excess parasitic drain, a good method is:
questions.explanation: Fuse voltage-drop or sequential fuse removal isolates the draining branch without waking modules where possible.

options.label: B
options.body: Measure voltage drop across fuses or pull fuses one at a time while watching draw fall

questions.prompt: A smart charger differs from a basic charger because it:
questions.explanation: Smart chargers bulk, absorb and float, and often have AGM/lithium modes and maintenance.

options.label: B
options.body: Uses multi-stage charging and can adapt rate and mode to battery condition and type

questions.prompt: Charging a deeply discharged AGM battery with the wrong mode may:
questions.explanation: Battery type settings matter; AGM and lithium have different voltage limits.

options.label: B
options.body: Undercharge it or damage it if voltage limits are wrong

questions.prompt: An alternator produces electricity by:
questions.explanation: The rotating rotor field induces AC in the stator, rectified to DC.

options.label: A
options.body: Spinning a magnetic field inside stationary stator windings

questions.prompt: The rectifier (diode pack) in an alternator:
questions.explanation: Diodes rectify stator AC into usable DC output.

options.label: A
options.body: Converts AC from the stator to DC for the vehicle

options.label: B
options.body: Converts DC to AC for the headlights

questions.prompt: The voltage regulator controls charging by:
questions.explanation: More field current makes a stronger field and higher output.

questions.prompt: Excessive AC ripple in alternator output most likely indicates:
questions.explanation: Failed diodes/windings let AC ripple through and reduce output.

options.label: A
options.body: A healthy diode pack in all cases

options.label: B
options.body: A faulty diode or stator winding

questions.prompt: Ripple can be checked with:
questions.explanation: A scope pattern or AC voltage measurement reveals abnormal ripple.

options.label: A
options.body: A scope on the output or a meter on AC volts

questions.prompt: If charging voltage is too high for a long period, a likely result is:
questions.explanation: Overvoltage damages the battery and sensitive electronics.

options.label: B
options.body: Battery overheating, gassing and damage to electronics

questions.prompt: A loose or slipping drive belt can cause:
questions.explanation: The alternator cannot reach required speed/output if the belt slips.

options.label: B
options.body: Low/intermittent charging, noise and battery warning under load

questions.prompt: A correct charging test sequence starts with:
questions.explanation: A weak battery or bad connection mimics alternator failure, so basics come first.

options.label: B
options.body: Checking battery condition, terminals, belt and grounds first

questions.prompt: Charging voltage on a conventional 12 V system at running idle is commonly about:
questions.explanation: Conventional systems regulate roughly in the mid-13 to mid-14 volt range; smart systems vary.

questions.prompt: Voltage drop testing the alternator output and ground paths under load finds:
questions.explanation: Loaded drop tests reveal cable and connection resistance between alternator and battery.

options.label: A
options.body: Only open circuits with no current

options.label: B
options.body: High resistance that a voltage-at-battery reading alone can hide

questions.prompt: In an ECM-controlled charging system, the module varies alternator output to:
questions.explanation: Smart control balances charge needs with engine load and emissions/economy targets.

options.label: B
options.body: Match electrical load, battery state, temperature and fuel-economy goals

questions.prompt: Smart charging may deliberately lower voltage during steady cruise because:
questions.explanation: Reducing field when charge is not needed cuts engine drag.

options.label: A
options.body: The battery is faulty in all such cases

options.label: B
options.body: A fully charged battery needs less, and reducing alternator load saves fuel

questions.prompt: During deceleration, some smart systems increase charging voltage to:
questions.explanation: Raising output on overrun uses vehicle momentum to recharge the battery.

options.label: A
options.body: Waste energy deliberately with no benefit

options.label: B
options.body: Recover energy (regenerative-style charging) while engine braking

questions.prompt: A battery current sensor on the negative lead allows the module to:
questions.explanation: Current, voltage and temperature data let the module estimate state of charge and health.

options.label: B
options.body: Monitor charge/discharge current to calculate battery state

questions.prompt: If the communication/control line to a smart alternator fails, many systems will:
questions.explanation: Most designs fail-safe to a conventional default voltage so the vehicle stays powered.

options.label: A
options.body: Stop charging forever in all designs

options.label: B
options.body: Default to a fixed fallback charging voltage

questions.prompt: When diagnosing smart charging, a measured 12.8 V while running does NOT automatically mean failure because:
questions.explanation: Commanded voltage varies; compare scan data, command and battery state before condemning parts.

options.label: B
options.body: The module may be intentionally commanding a lower voltage at that moment

options.label: D
options.body: Alternators do not charge at idle

questions.prompt: The first scan-tool checks for a smart charging complaint should include:
questions.explanation: Desired vs actual generator data shows whether control or the alternator is at fault.

options.label: A
options.body: Only fault codes for the radio

options.label: B
options.body: Battery state data, commanded/desired voltage, generator feedback and related codes

questions.prompt: After replacing a battery on a smart charging vehicle, you may need to:
questions.explanation: Battery registration resets learned age/type data; without it charging can be wrong.

options.label: B
options.body: Register/reset the battery monitoring system so charging adapts to the new battery

questions.prompt: A faulty battery temperature or current sensor input can cause:
questions.explanation: Bad inputs lead the module to command inappropriate charging.

options.label: B
options.body: Incorrect charging voltage decisions and warning lights

questions.prompt: A voltage drop in the alternator ground on a smart system can cause:
questions.explanation: Ground resistance affects both output and sensing, mimicking alternator failure.

options.label: B
options.body: The module to misread or the alternator to undercharge despite a good unit

questions.prompt: The starter solenoid has two main jobs:
questions.explanation: The solenoid shifts the pinion into mesh and switches heavy motor current.

options.label: A
options.body: Charge the battery and run the lights

options.label: B
options.body: Engage the pinion with the ring gear and close the motor contacts

options.label: D
options.body: Cool the motor and time the spark

questions.prompt: A single click and no crank most often points to:
questions.explanation: The signal is arriving (click) but heavy current is not turning the motor.

options.label: B
options.body: Poor heavy-current contacts, low battery, bad connections or a seized/faulty motor - not the signal alone

questions.prompt: In a DC starter motor, torque is produced by:
questions.explanation: Current in the armature and field creates magnetic forces that rotate the armature.

options.label: A
options.body: Magnetic interaction between armature and field windings/coils

questions.prompt: Worn brushes or a dirty commutator in a DC motor cause:
questions.explanation: Poor brush contact interrupts armature current.

options.label: B
options.body: Intermittent or no operation and arcing

questions.prompt: Starter circuit voltage drop tests are done:
questions.explanation: High starter current reveals resistance; drops are measured during cranking.

options.label: A
options.body: With the circuit disconnected and an ohmmeter

options.label: B
options.body: While cranking, measuring across each cable and connection

questions.prompt: A 0.9 V drop across the positive starter cable while cranking indicates:
questions.explanation: That drop is far above a healthy cable's small drop under cranking load.

options.label: B
options.body: Excessive resistance in that cable or its connections

questions.prompt: Total starter circuit drop (positive plus ground) should generally be:
questions.explanation: Excess total drop starves the starter of voltage; always compare with manufacturer specs.

options.label: B
options.body: Kept low - typically under about 0.5 V total in a healthy system (check specifications)

options.label: D
options.body: Ignored if the engine starts once

questions.prompt: Start-stop vehicles need enhanced batteries (AGM/EFB) because they must handle:
questions.explanation: Start-stop duty cycles a normal flooded battery too hard, shortening its life.

options.label: B
options.body: Frequent restarts and deeper cycling while supporting loads engine-off

questions.prompt: A start-stop system will typically inhibit auto-stop when:
questions.explanation: Inhibit conditions protect battery, emissions, comfort and safety.

options.label: A
options.body: The cabin is at a comfortable temperature and battery is full in all cases

options.label: B
options.body: Battery state is low, engine is cold, or a large electrical/HVAC load demands the engine

options.label: C
options.body: The vehicle is stopped at lights with all conditions met

options.label: D
options.body: The brake pedal is pressed normally

questions.prompt: On restart, a start-stop system needs:
questions.explanation: Reinforced starters, suitable batteries and control logic make restarts quick and reliable.

options.label: A
options.body: A conventional slow crank with no support

options.label: B
options.body: A starter/battery and management system designed for fast, repeated restarts

options.label: C
options.body: The driver to use a hand crank

questions.prompt: Low-speed / fault-tolerant CAN is typically used for:
questions.explanation: Low-speed CAN suits doors, seats, lighting and other body systems.

options.label: A
options.body: Engine torque control at the fastest rates

options.label: B
options.body: Body and comfort functions where speed is less critical

questions.prompt: A feature of fault-tolerant low-speed CAN is that it can:
questions.explanation: Fault-tolerant transceivers can operate single-wire in limited faults.

options.label: B
options.body: Continue communicating on one wire in some fault conditions

questions.prompt: High-speed CAN uses two wires, CAN-H and CAN-L, which carry:
questions.explanation: Differential signalling rejects common-mode noise.

options.label: B
options.body: Differential signals that are mirror images, improving noise immunity

options.label: C
options.body: One power and one ground only

questions.prompt: With the system off, resistance between CAN-H and CAN-L on a healthy terminated high-speed bus is about:
questions.explanation: Two 120-ohm terminators in parallel measure about 60 ohms.

options.label: C
options.body: 120 ohms only at one end measured alone on the bus

questions.prompt: If CAN-H is shorted to ground, the likely result is:
questions.explanation: A short collapses differential signalling and modules cannot communicate reliably.

options.label: B
options.body: Loss or severe disruption of communication on that bus

questions.prompt: FlexRay was designed for:
questions.explanation: FlexRay provides time-determined, redundant communication for critical systems.

options.label: B
options.body: Deterministic, high-speed, fault-tolerant communication for chassis/safety systems

questions.prompt: A key FlexRay concept is:
questions.explanation: Time-triggered slots guarantee when critical messages are sent.

options.label: A
options.body: Messages sent only when a switch is pressed, with no timing

options.label: B
options.body: Static time slots in a repeating cycle for guaranteed message timing

questions.prompt: MOST bus is a network mainly used for:
questions.explanation: MOST carries audio, video and infotainment data around a ring.

options.label: B
options.body: Infotainment / multimedia data, often over optical fibre

questions.prompt: In a MOST ring, an open or broken fibre at one point will:
questions.explanation: A ring break stops data circulating past the break.

options.label: B
options.body: Interrupt the ring and can take down the infotainment network

questions.prompt: LIN bus is best described as:
questions.explanation: LIN handles simple body slaves under a master module at low cost.

options.label: B
options.body: A low-cost single-wire sub-bus where a master controls slave nodes such as switches, motors and sensors
